title: Wigwagonock (Sag Harbor)
summary: Wigwagonock is a Sag Harbor placename associated with land east of Division Street and an Indigenous village site near Sleight's Hill.
introduction_content: Wigwagonock, also written Wegwagonuck, Wegwaganuck, and Wegwagonock, names the part of Sag Harbor east of Division Street in East Hampton town.
history_content:
The placename is connected with an Indigenous village site marked by a large shell heap near the foot of Sleight's Hill. Local land records use related spellings in connection with meadows and common lands around Sag Harbor.

A port connected to global Shinnecock whaling

Sag Harbor was one starting point in a much larger Shinnecock maritime history. As the local industry declined, experienced Shinnecock whalers found work through New London, New Bedford, and San Francisco and sailed throughout the Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic. The story of the Amethyst, lost in 1885 with Moses Walker, Ferdinand Lee, and Garrison Lee aboard, makes the global reach and danger of that work visible. See Whaling.1
translation_content:
The name is interpreted as "land or place at the end of the hill," connecting its elements with words for "end," "hill," and "place."

Why Place Names Matter

“Naming who you are and where you come from is essential to Indigenous communities.”

— Angelo Baca, The Power of ‘Bears Ears’ and Indigenous Place Names (2018), article body, ‘What’s in a name?’
preservation_content: Wigwagonock connects a Sag Harbor neighborhood, a documented village site, and colonial-era land records. Exact boundaries and excavation locations are not identified.
whereintheworld_content: Approximate blue/general placement east of Division Street in Sag Harbor, near the described Sleight's Hill area. Coordinates are approximate and not exact historic coordinates.
